strengths: Well-motivated core contribution addressing verifier-free test-time scaling for diffusion models with clear System 2 thinking analogy
Novel LRNCL loss that intuitively enforces performance-energy consistency through linear regression on negative samples
Strong empirical results demonstrating impressive out-of-distribution generalization (88% on 15×15 Maze when trained on 6×6; 43% vs 30% on harder Sudoku)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with detailed ablations isolating contributions of each component and ground-truth oracle comparisons providing useful upper bounds
Solid presentation with clear motivation, well-designed figures (especially Figure 2 overview), detailed reproducibility information including training times and computational resources
Reasonable hybrid approach (hMCTS) combining best-of-N exploration with MCTS refinement, with clear motivation for why pure BoN plateaus
weaknesses: Very limited evaluation scope: only two highly structured combinatorial puzzle tasks (Maze and Sudoku); unclear generalization to other reasoning domains or real-world applications
Energy function design appears task-specific (L2 norm of predictions); lacks guidance on designing energy functions for new domains and may not generalize beyond structured reasoning

LRNCL design choices insufficiently justified: use of linear regression justified only in footnote 8 as future work; no ablations on number of negatives or hyperparameter γ; negative sample generation via permutation noise is task-specific

Significant training overhead (3× increase: 2h→6h for Maze, 4h→7h for Sudoku) introduced to enable test-time scaling, but no analysis of training cost vs. performance trade-off or practical implications

hMCTS has notable limitations: MCTS start step ts requires careful tuning (Table 10, Fig. 8 show sensitivity peaks); limited parallel computing compatibility (acknowledged but unaddressed); constraint K=Nr=L seems artificial
No statistical significance testing: no error bars, confidence intervals, or variance across runs; test sets are relatively small making single-point estimates unreliable
Missing comparisons with other recent test-time scaling methods for diffusion models despite citing relevant work (Ma et al. 2025); primarily compared only against single baseline (Du et al. 2024)

Limited theoretical justification: no explanation for why LRNCL specifically improves energy landscapes; no analysis of how energy landscape changes during training; relationship between performance-energy consistency and actual scaling only empirically demonstrated

Performance-energy consistency metric achieves only ~84% even with full training, suggesting energy function remains imperfect verifier; consistency metric is essentially Kendall's τ (not novel) and sufficiency threshold is not justified

Generalization assumptions not addressed: both tasks are deterministic with ground-truth solutions; unclear if approach works for stochastic or less-structured domains where lower energy may not correlate with quality

strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing the gap between external and intrinsic verifiers for test-time scaling
Comprehensive ablation studies (Sections 5.1-5.3) that systematically diagnose bottlenecks and validate each component
Strong empirical results on Maze tasks with impressive out-of-distribution generalization (88% on 15×15 trained on 6×6)
Extensive experimental details, hyperparameters, and reproducibility information in appendices
Well-structured presentation with clear figures and organized methodology
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only two highly similar combinatorial tasks (Maze and Sudoku); no evidence of generalization to other reasoning domains

LRNCL loss design appears ad-hoc: linear regression assumption between energy and L2 distance is restrictive and unjustified; only 3 points per sample is statistically fragile; multiple unconstrained loss terms without clear weighting

Incremental novelty: LRNCL is a contrastive learning variant, KL regularization directly from [20], hMCTS is straightforward application of MCTS to diffusion; components are largely combinations of existing techniques

Energy landscape analysis is superficial: 'performance-energy consistency' is merely Spearman rank correlation; root causes of poor energy functions never deeply analyzed; Figure 4 shows improvement but absolute L2 distances remain high

hMCTS method sensitivity and limitations: Appendix D shows dramatic performance variation with MCTS start step ts (significant peak at specific values, sharp drops elsewhere); no computational timing analysis; modest 5% improvement on Sudoku suggests limited generality

Experimental setup limitations: artificial distribution shift (6×6→15×15); missing comparisons with recent test-time scaling methods [6,17] and alternative planning algorithms; no error bars or statistical significance testing
Overclaimed generality: claims about 'intrinsic reasoning' and 'System 2 thinking' not well-supported given narrow task scope; task-specific design choices (permutation noise) unlikely to transfer
Insufficient justification for KL regularization: why maximize entropy in constrained reasoning where incorrect diverse samples are useless? Mechanism unexplained

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies the gap of test-time scaling for diffusion models without external verifiers and articulates two specific technical challenges
Novel performance-energy consistency concept: The insight that energy should align with solution quality is valuable, with a useful quantitative metric
Solid technical contributions: LRNCL loss for regularizing relative energy ordering of negatives and hMCTS for efficient search are reasonable solutions
Thorough experimental validation: Comprehensive ablation studies clearly show the contribution of each component; systematic analysis of bottlenecks
Convincing empirical results: Dramatic generalization improvements (88% on 15×15 Maze vs 0% baseline) demonstrate practical effectiveness
Good presentation and reproducibility: Clear figures, detailed algorithms, comprehensive hyperparameters, and extensive appendices facilitate reproduction
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: Only two discrete optimization tasks (Maze, Sudoku) tested; no evaluation on other reasoning domains (math, symbolic reasoning, planning, etc.); generalizability claims unsupported
Energy as verifier remains fragile: Performance-energy consistency only reaches ~84% even with LRNCL; 16% ranking disagreement with actual performance; requires substantial engineering to barely work

LRNCL design is ad-hoc: Linear relationship enforcement lacks justification (why not more complex shapes?); L2 distance as quality proxy unvalidated; slope parameter γ requires tuning without clear guidance

hMCTS requires careful tuning: Switching parameter t_s shows high sensitivity (performance ranges 0.078-0.797); no principled way to choose t_s for new problems; limited analysis of why hybrid is better than pure MCTS
Significant computational overhead: Training time triples with full VFScale; MCTS has poor parallelization (acknowledged but unresolved); test-time cost analysis missing
Limited baseline comparisons: No direct comparison with other test-time scaling methods [6,17]; only compared against single baseline [5]; missing pure MCTS or other search variants

Oversold 'intrinsic reasoning' framing: Requires carefully designed LRNCL loss and task-specific hyperparameter tuning (γ, t_s, c, noise scales); distinction from external verifier is philosophical rather than fundamental
Task-specific negative sampling: Generalization to other domains unclear; permutation noise strategy not validated across different problem types
Missing technical analysis: No error analysis, failure case studies, or investigation of which problem types benefit most; hyperparameter c=100 chosen without ablation

strengths: Clear problem identification and thorough diagnostic analysis showing that performance-energy consistency (~70%) is a bottleneck for test-time scaling
Novel MRNCL training objective that effectively aligns energy with solution quality through linear regression on triplet constraints
Strong empirical results within demonstrated scope: 88% success on 15×15 Maze (trained on 6×6) vs. near-zero baseline, with consistent improvements on Sudoku
Rigorous experimental methodology with fair comparisons (identical NFE), comprehensive ablations (Tables 1,3,4), multi-seed stability, and sensitivity analyses

Valuable analyses including comparison to oracle verifiers (Table 11) showing intrinsic energy achieves near-oracle performance, and demonstration that external verifiers with high statistical correlation fail at selection
Comprehensive appendix and reproducible code supporting reproducibility and detailed experimental transparency
weaknesses: Critical limitation: evaluation restricted to only 2 synthetic, discrete, grid-based tasks with easily verifiable ground truth; no evaluation on other reasoning domains (arithmetic, logic, non-spatial reasoning) raises serious generalization concerns

Linear relationship assumption in MRNCL not rigorously justified: Table 12 shows QRNCL achieves better N=1 performance, suggesting linearity may be suboptimal; connection from local triplet constraints to global ranking (Section D.6) asserted via empirical success rather than proven

Energy function quality remains sub-optimal: 84% performance-energy consistency (Table 4) implies 16% ranking errors; Kendall-τ correlations (Table 19) are modest (0.40-0.48) at critical denoising steps; unclear if this represents high quality or fundamental limitation

hMCTS design lacks justification: why does pure MCTS perform poorly (Table 5) despite good training? No ablation of the specific hybrid strategy (early BoN + late MCTS); limited theoretical or intuitive explanation beyond empirical observation

Significant practical costs inadequately weighed: training time 3× increase (2h→6h), peak memory 7× increase (3.4GB→23.05GB for Maze), inference 31% overhead (Table 23)—prohibitive for many users and not adequately justified against performance gains

Negative sample generation is task-specific (permutation noise for grids): generalization to non-spatial reasoning unclear; Table 17 shows Gaussian noise substantially underperforms, raising concerns about applicability to other domains

Incomplete verifier analysis: only compares to one trained external verifier; doesn't rule out that better verifier training strategies could close the gap; limited engagement with reward model training literature
Limited baseline comparisons: only compares against Du et al. (2024); missing comparisons with other test-time scaling methods and alternative MCTS formulations

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies the gap between external verifiers (hard to train) and intrinsic reasoning
Thorough experimental analysis within scope: strong ablations, multi-seed stability, oracle comparisons demonstrate rigor
Clear bottleneck identification: Section 5.1 effectively separates training-side (energy landscape) vs inference-side (search efficiency) issues
Strong empirical results on tested domains: 88% success on 15×15 mazes vs 6% baseline is impressive
Reproducibility: comprehensive appendix, promised code release, extensive implementation details
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only 2 synthetic, grid-based reasoning tasks (Maze, Sudoku) with no evidence of generalization to SAT, graphs, or other domains—insufficient for top-tier venue
Misleading 'verifier-free' framing: the energy function is a learned verifier; the novelty is joint training (intrinsic) not elimination of verification—this misrepresents the contribution

Incremental technical novelty: MRNCL is straightforward contrastive learning + linear regression; KL regularization reused from prior work; hMCTS is a simple BoN→MCTS hybrid without strong justification

Weak theoretical justification: why should enforcing local linear monotonicity between 3 samples lead to globally aligned energy? Connection relies entirely on empirical results rather than principled reasoning

Circular validation logic: paper optimizes for performance-energy consistency then validates using it; while oracle comparisons (Table 11) provide some external validation, core argument is somewhat circular
Significant computational overhead under-acknowledged: 3× training time increase (Maze), 31% inference time overhead (hMCTS vs BoN)—cost-benefit analysis missing

Design choices appear task-specific: permutation-based negative sampling, discrete-continuous-discrete pipeline, hyperparameter values (c=100) seem tailored to Maze/Sudoku without evidence of portability
N=1 performance degradation: VFScale underperforms single-shot generation (Tables 1, 3), suggesting the method trades one compute regime for another rather than uniformly improving
Incomplete comparison to external verifiers: only one trained classifier tested; unclear if better-tuned external verifiers would perform differently or if the training setup was equivalent
hMCTS design appears ad-hoc: no justification for why BoN→MCTS specifically; no ablations comparing to other hybrid strategies; adaptive t_s only provides modest improvements (Table 13)
Missing recent baselines: no comparison to Ma et al. (2025), Yoon et al. (2025), or other concurrent test-time scaling methods
Limited analysis of failure modes and problem characteristics: when/why does the method fail? What problem structure makes it harder/easier?
No evidence of cross-domain generalization: only same 2 domains with OOD difficulty; no Maze→Sudoku or Sudoku→SAT type evaluation
Overstated claims: 'intrinsic reasoning' and 'System 2 thinking' analogies are loose; calling it 'scalable' based on 2 synthetic tasks is strong language

strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying two specific challenges (energy landscape quality and search efficiency) with principled solutions
Novel MRNCL loss effectively enforcing performance-energy consistency through well-designed monotonic regression objective
Strong experimental results showing substantial improvements on tested tasks (Maze: 6% → 88%; Sudoku: 9% → 43% OOD)
Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 1, 3, 5, 12) rigorously isolating contributions of each component
Thorough empirical analysis including comparison with ground truth oracles (Table 11) validating learned energy quality and stability analysis over 10 seeds (Table 18)
Fair experimental methodology with identical NFE allocation across compared methods ensuring valid search strategy comparison
Good reproducibility with promised code release and detailed hyperparameters in appendices
Insightful trade-off analysis between single-sample performance and test-time scalability (Section 5.2)
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: only two synthetic discrete optimization tasks (Maze and Sudoku); no evaluation on other reasoning domains (planning, theorem proving, arithmetic, visual reasoning) or continuous problems, fundamentally limiting generalizability claims
Modest out-of-distribution generalization: Maze 6×6→15×15 (2.5× scale) and Sudoku 33→17 digits are relatively small shifts; no extreme generalization tests
Limited comparison with alternative approaches: only baseline is Du et al. (2024); missing comparisons with other test-time scaling methods and search algorithms

Unclear theoretical justification for local-to-global consistency: MRNCL enforces monotonicity on only triplets of samples; while D.6 provides empirical evidence (Kendall-τ in Table 19), principled theoretical argument is absent
Substantial computational overhead: training time 2h→6h (3×), memory 3.4GB→23GB (6.8×), inference wall-clock 31% overhead; costs may be prohibitive for practical applications
hMCTS introduces new hyperparameters requiring tuning (especially switch-over step t_s in Figure 8); less parallelizable than BoN limiting scalability

Energy function dependency: framework assumes energy can be shaped as good verifier; gap remains between learned energy and perfect oracle (Table 11); no analysis of failure modes or problem types where approach struggles

Design choices lack sufficient justification: linear regression for MRNCL feels somewhat arbitrary (though D.2 provides ablation); choice of permutation noise for discrete tasks justified post-hoc; only 3 data points for line fitting is sparse
Limited novelty: contributions are somewhat incremental over Du et al. (2024)—essentially two auxiliary losses plus hybrid search applied to their framework
Missing critical analysis: no discussion of failure modes, solution quality-budget tradeoffs, or problem characteristics favoring this approach; no error analysis beyond aggregate metrics
